When the first reducer would not back-drive

My early cycloidal actuator had a mechanical-efficiency problem: it resisted back-driving instead of behaving like a responsive robot joint.

That made a distinction clear. A reducer could assemble and turn under motor power while still creating too much resistance for the joint behavior I wanted. I needed to investigate the load path and losses, rather than judge the design only by its reduction ratio.

Start with the disk, pins, and bearing stack

I parameterized the cycloidal disk and pin geometry in SolidWorks, then worked through eccentricity, shaft and bearing support, output interfaces, and the printed housing. Repeated prototypes made fits and assembly behavior visible.

Useful output depends on the losses
ωout = ωmotor / G
τout ≈ ηGτmotor
η = Pout / Pin

G is the reduction ratio. Efficiency η must be measured at a stated operating point. Forward efficiency and back-driving behavior are related design concerns, but one does not establish the other.

What I changed and investigated

  1. Prototype loop

    Revisit fit and mechanical support

    I revisited clearances, bearing selection and support, print orientation, and mechanical interfaces. The assembly review also flagged tight fits and binding risk. These were practical candidates to investigate, rather than proof of a single confirmed loss mechanism.

  2. Packaging revisions

    Make room for the electronics and the assembly process

    The CAD evolved around the controller board, bearings, output flange, and motor package. The project review also identified heat near printed material, airflow, wiring routes, and fastener access.

  3. Documented reducer variants

    Compare the 17:1 and 25:1 designs

    The original 17:1 design was retained in the repository but is no longer maintained. The revised 25:1 assembly changes the reduction and output-shaft sleeve bearing. This revision targets torque margin; it is not, by itself, evidence that back-driving or efficiency improved.

Reduction also changes reflected inertia
Jmotor → output = G²Jmotor
Jload → motor = Jload / G²

These ideal relations help explain why torque multiplication, responsiveness, and back-driving need to be considered together. A higher ratio is not a universal improvement.

Build a way to measure the next revision

I developed a dynamometer layout and fixture tests to investigate torque, efficiency, backlash, repeatability, and temperature rise. Comparing revisions requires the same speed, load, warm-up state, and measurement method.

The retained plots do not establish a calibrated back-drive breakaway torque or a before-and-after efficiency rating for an identified pair of revisions. I therefore keep the observed early problem separate from performance that still needs a controlled comparison.

The actuation question carried forward

WHAT THIS ESTABLISHES

From printed cycloidal prototypes toward a different actuation tradeoff.

Cycloidal prototypes were integrated into the robot. The later planetary QDD study explores lower reduction and different packaging. Its CAD is a design study, with physical performance still to be established.
